title: Checkout Latency with JDBC Pool Saturation
simulationLabel: Deterministic synthetic Dynatrace-style traces, metrics, logs, and commerce outcomes; no live SAP Commerce Cloud environment is accessed.
brief: Checkout p95 rose from 1.8 seconds to 18.6 seconds during peak traffic. Errors report timeouts waiting for database connections. Heap is elevated but stable. Diagnose the shared bottleneck, contain impact safely, and prove recovery.

initialState.businessImpact: 31% checkout failure rate; browsing remains available

investigations.label: Inspect checkout latency, errors, traffic, and business success

evidence.observation: Latency and failures rise without a material traffic increase.

investigations.label: Review deployments, configuration, and workload events

events.event: No application deployment or property change

evidence.observation: A manually started custom workload precedes degradation; this is correlation, not yet proof.

investigations.label: Compare JVM, GC, CPU, and worker indicators

evidence.finding: No memory or CPU saturation precedes the incident. API workers are mostly waiting, so JVM pressure is not established as the primary cause.

investigations.label: Inspect JDBC connection-pool use and wait time by service

evidence.finding: Both services approach their configured pool ceiling and connection-borrow wait tracks checkout latency.

investigations.label: Trace slow checkout requests and database backtraces

databaseBacktrace.queryPattern: SELECT customer export projection in pages
databaseBacktrace.observation: No single slow query dominates; high parallel query volume holds pooled connections.

investigations.label: Inspect custom export execution and ownership

evidence.finding: The custom job was manually started without an explicit node group and opens overlapping read transactions. The simulation models customer code behavior, not an SAP-delivered job.

investigations.label: Check order and payment state around timeouts

evidence.finding: Three authorizations need controlled reconciliation; blind client retries could duplicate side effects.

investigations.label: Correlate timeout logs to traces and job execution

events.message: Timeout waiting for idle database connection

evidence.privacy: Synthetic identifiers contain no customer data.

actions.label: Assign incident command, freeze nonessential jobs, and set update cadence
actions.outcome: Ownership and communication cadence are established.
actions.consequence: Further nonessential workload changes require incident approval.

actions.label: Abort the customer-owned export job through the supported administration path
actions.outcome: The abortable custom export stops opening new transactions.
actions.consequence: Existing requests drain; checkout recovery is not assumed until independently measured.

actions.label: Apply the documented application-level duplicate-submission guard and customer messaging
actions.outcome: Ambiguous retries are contained and customers receive bounded failure guidance.
actions.consequence: New duplicate side effects are reduced while reconciliation continues.

actions.label: Run synthetic checkout, pool-drain, latency, error-rate, and order/payment reconciliation checks
actions.outcome: Pool use returns below 55%, checkout p95 returns below 2.2 seconds, errors fall below 1%, and three payment exceptions enter controlled reconciliation.
actions.consequence: Service returns to monitored operation; the export remains disabled pending engineering repair.

stateChanges.businessImpact: Recovered; three payment exceptions under reconciliation

actions.label: Restart every application service immediately
actions.outcome: The simulator records an unsafe symptom-reset decision.
actions.consequence: Active requests are disrupted and the export workload resumes without removing the cause.

stateChanges.businessImpact: Checkout disruption extended by indiscriminate restart

actions.label: Double the production JDBC pool without database capacity evidence
actions.outcome: The simulator blocks unreviewed capacity transfer to the managed database.
actions.consequence: More concurrent queries could amplify database contention; the custom workload remains defective.

actions.label: Directly terminate database sessions on the managed database
actions.outcome: The simulator blocks an unsupported direct-database action.
actions.consequence: Direct managed-database intervention requires SAP Support and a justified recovery request.

sequence.prompt: Define the affected journey and compare latency, errors, throughput, and business success in one time window.
Build a change-and-workload timeline. Which event precedes degradation, and what evidence would keep it from becoming a correlation fallacy?
Test the JVM hypothesis with heap, GC, CPU, and worker states. Which signal moved first?
Check whether request waiting aligns with JDBC pool occupancy and borrow latency by service.
Use a request trace and database backtrace to locate where checkout time is spent and which caller drives database work.
Establish whether the workload is SAP-delivered or customer-developed, how it started, where it runs, and whether it can be stopped safely.
Before mitigation, quantify ambiguous order and payment outcomes so retries do not create duplicate effects.
Choose the smallest reversible action that removes the evidenced source while preserving managed-platform boundaries.
Define recovery using both technical saturation signals and independently observed checkout and transaction outcomes.

tutor.conclusionPrompt: State the timeline, competing hypotheses, evidence-led cause, containment, transaction protection, recovery proof, ownership boundary, and durable prevention.
tutor.uncertainty: All evidence values are synthetic. SAP documentation supports the investigation methods and responsibility boundaries, not these invented incident measurements.

solution.rootCause: A manually started customer-developed export CronJob used excessive parallel database work, saturating JDBC pools and making checkout workers wait for connections. Heap, GC, and CPU were secondary observations, not the leading cause.
solution.recovery: Declare the incident, abort the customer-owned job through supported administration, protect ambiguous checkout retries, allow existing requests to drain, verify pool use and checkout SLIs, reconcile payment/order exceptions, then redesign and load-test export concurrency, scheduling, node-group behavior, and alerts.
